column1: #meta label(flipped_halls) message(Carve four L shaped halls in one pass
column2: each the same room in a different orientation. Place the cursor at the top-left corner and leave a clear 12 by 12 area; the second copy is rotated
column3: the third and fourth are mirrored
column4: and each is shifted six tiles from the first so they do not overlap.)

column1: tags: meta, dig, transform, mirror, rotate

description: A #meta blueprint that stamps one asymmetric #dig room four times with transform() so each copy is a different orientation of the same shape. The referenced /hall_wing is an L: a short vertical arm two tiles tall and a long horizontal arm four tiles wide
column2: so it has no symmetry to hide behind. Because the shape is asymmetric
column3: a rotate or a mirror visibly changes the FOOTPRINT itself
column4: not just a facing direction. transform(rotcw) rotates the room 90 degrees clockwise (its bounding box turns from two tall by four wide into four tall by two wide). transform(fliph) mirrors it left to right
column5: and transform(flipv) mirrors it up to down
column6: so the L corner lands in a different spot in each copy. Transforms in one call are applied in order and are space separated with no comma
column7: so a CSV cell does not split them. Each reference also carries a shift() to slide its copy six tiles from the first (six right
column10: laying the four halls in a 2x2 arrangement without overlapping; when both markers are on one reference the shift is applied AFTER the transform. This is the corpus's first transform() on an ASYMMETRIC footprint
column11: and its first fliph and flipv demonstration: meta-rotated-gates.csv names fliph and flipv but uses a symmetric 3x3 square
column12: where a flip leaves the shape unchanged and only the machinery direction moves
column13: so the mirror itself is invisible there. Here the shape does the moving. Where meta-residential-tower.csv uses repeat(down 5) to stack a floor down the Z-axis and meta-tiled-quarters.csv uses shift() to spread copies across one floor
column14: this uses transform() to reorient them. This blueprint deliberately omits start() on the #dig room: without a start() marker Quickfort anchors the room at its top-left corner
column15: so the four orientations read unambiguously against the cursor. Combining start() with transform() on an asymmetric footprint is the subtle anchor case to check in-game (the case the symmetric-square rotated-gates example sidestepped); add a start() only once you have confirmed where the cursor lands after each rotation. The room is dug with plain d mine tokens
column16: so carve a corridor of your own to link the four halls.
